content: Burn injuries are a significant health concern, with the head and neck region being particularly vulnerable. The face, as a central aspect of personal identity and communication, is often affected. Topical treatments are the primary approach for managing facial burns. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of various topical interventions on wound healing in individuals with facial burns of any depth. A comprehensive search was conducted in December 2019 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, and EBSCO CINAHL Plus. Clinical trial registries were also reviewed for ongoing and unpublished studies, and reference lists of relevant studies, reviews, and meta-analyses were examined. No restrictions were applied regarding language, publication date, or study setting. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the effects of topical treatments for facial burns were included. Two independent reviewers handled study selection, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, and evaluation of evidence certainty using the GRADE approach. This updated review included 12 RCTs involving 507 participants, primarily adults treated in specialized burn centers. The topical agents studied included antimicrobial agents (e.g., silver sulfadiazine (SSD), Aquacel-Ag, cerium-sulfadiazine, gentamicin cream, mafenide acetate cream, bacitracin), non-antimicrobial agents (e.g., Moist Exposed Burn Ointment (MEBO), saline-soaked dressings, skin substitutes like TransCyte, allografts, and porcine Xenoderm), and other treatments (e.g., growth hormone therapy, recombinant human granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor hydrogel (rhGMCS), enzymatic debridement, and Helix Aspersa extract cream). However, the evidence was predominantly of low or very low certainty due to high risks of bias, unclear randomization methods, lack of blinding, and imprecision caused by small sample sizes or low event rates. Comparison of Antimicrobial and Non-Antimicrobial Agents: Moderate-certainty evidence suggests little to no difference in time to complete wound healing between antimicrobial agents (e.g., SSD) and non-antimicrobial agents (e.g., MEBO) (hazard ratio (HR) 0.84, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.85; 1 study, 39 participants). Low-certainty evidence indicates that antimicrobial agents may have little to no effect on the proportion of completely healed wounds compared to non-antimicrobial agents (risk ratio (RR) 0.94, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.29; 1 study, 39 participants). Very low-certainty evidence leaves uncertainty about differences in wound infection rates between antimicrobial agents (e.g., Aquacel-Ag) and non-antimicrobial agents (e.g., MEBO) (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.21; 1 study, 40 participants). No data were available on changes in wound surface area or partial wound healing. Scar quality and patient satisfaction were assessed with low-certainty evidence, and pain outcomes were incompletely reported. Comparison of Different Antimicrobial Agents: Low-certainty evidence suggests uncertainty regarding differences in time to partial wound healing (e.g., SSD vs. cerium SSD: mean difference (MD) –7.10 days, 95% CI –16.43 to 2.23; 1 study, 142 participants). Very low-certainty evidence exists for differences in wound infection rates (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.17; 1 study, 15 participants). Evidence for other outcomes, such as the need for surgery, pain, scar quality, adverse effects, and hospital stay duration, was of low to very low certainty. Comparison of Skin Substitutes and Antimicrobial Agents: Low-certainty evidence suggests that skin substitutes may slightly reduce time to partial wound healing compared to unspecified antimicrobial agents (MD –6.00 days, 95% CI –8.69 to –3.31; 1 study, 34 participants). Very low-certainty evidence leaves uncertainty about other outcomes, including wound infection, pain, scar quality, adverse effects, and hospital stay duration. A bioengineered skin substitute may slightly reduce procedural pain (MD –4.00, 95% CI –5.05 to –2.95; 34 participants) and background pain (MD –2.00, 95% CI –3.05 to –0.95; 34 participants) compared to an unspecified antimicrobial agent. Conversely, a biological dressing (porcine Xenoderm) might slightly increase pain in superficial burns (MD 1.20, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.75; 15 participants) and deep partial-thickness burns (MD 3.00, 95% CI 2.34 to 3.66; 10 participants) compared to antimicrobial agents (Physiotulle Ag). Comparison of Miscellaneous Treatments: Low-certainty evidence suggests that MEBO may slightly reduce time to complete wound healing compared to saline-soaked dressings (MD –1.7 days, 95% CI –3.32 to –0.08; 40 participants). A cream containing Helix Aspersa extract may slightly increase the proportion of wounds completely healed at 14 days compared to MEBO (RR 4.77, 95% CI 1.87 to 12.15; 43 participants). Very low-certainty evidence leaves uncertainty about differences in wound infection, scar quality, pain, and patient satisfaction for other miscellaneous treatments. Conclusions: The evidence regarding the effects of topical interventions for facial burns is predominantly of low to very low certainty. While the number of RCTs in burn care is increasing, the overall quality of evidence remains limited due to methodological shortcomings and insufficient adherence to evidence-based standards in study design and reporting.
